evals.prompt: I've spent two months researching a real corporate accounting scandal from the 90s (SEC filings, deposition transcripts, a couple of retrospective journalism pieces) because I want to write a novel loosely based on it. I have a folder full of PDFs and a rough idea that my protagonist should be a junior auditor who starts noticing irregularities. But every time I try to start writing, I end up just narrating what actually happened instead of it feeling like a story. Where do I even start?
evals.expected_output: Assistant should recognize this as a research-to-architecture transition rather than a research-organization problem alone. It should push the user toward a project contract (what should this do to a reader) and dramatic architecture questions (character desire/need, antagonistic force, information asymmetry, causality, the 'if this scene disappears what becomes impossible' test) rather than just proposing an outline or a research-filing system. It should also raise the idea that some research findings should deliberately never appear on the page (the fourth research bucket), since 'narrating what actually happened' is a classic symptom of that distinction being skipped. It should not immediately start drafting prose for the user.
assertions: Response addresses what effect the story should have on the reader or the project's guiding question (a project-contract-style question), not just structural/outlining advice
Response explicitly raises dramatic-architecture concepts: character desire/need, an antagonistic force, or causality between events -- not just "make an outline"
Response distinguishes categories of research findings, including the idea that some researched material should deliberately never appear in the book
Response does not immediately write example prose or a draft scene for the user unprompted
Response poses some version of a scene/beat-necessity test (e.g. "if this scene were cut, what becomes impossible later")

evals.prompt: Here's a scene I wrote: my main character Mara is having dinner with her dad and he mentions, almost in passing, that her mother had an affair years ago that Mara never knew about. I wrote three drafts and it still reads like it's just there to deliver the plot twist -- like a Wikipedia summary with dialogue tags. Can you help me figure out what's actually wrong with it, not just rewrite it for me?
evals.expected_output: Assistant should diagnose rather than immediately rewrite, honoring the user's explicit request. It should apply something like the information audit (distinguishing information necessary to the author vs. the character vs. the reader) to explain why the scene reads as expository, and/or raise character questions (what does the father want in this specific scene, what is he refusing to see, why is he revealing this now under what pressure) rather than treating the scene purely as an information-delivery problem. It should not simply hand back a polished rewritten version without first locating what's actually not working.
assertions: Response does not simply hand back a rewritten version of the scene without first diagnosing the problem, honoring the user's explicit request
Response distinguishes information the author needs to track vs. what the character would know vs. what the reader needs, in some functionally equivalent form

Response asks or raises a specific question about the father character's motivation, pressure, or reason for revealing this now, rather than treating the scene purely as an information-delivery mechanism
Response names the scene's failure mode specifically (e.g. exposition-dump, plot-delivery-only) rather than only giving generic advice like "show don't tell"

evals.prompt: I think my novel might be done? I've read it through twice and keep tweaking the same paragraph in chapter 3 every time -- small word changes, nothing major, but I've done it like eight times now. I gave it to four friends. Two said they loved the pacing in the second half. One said the villain's motivation didn't really make sense to her. Another said, and I quote, 'idk something about chapter 7 just felt off to me but I can't say what.' A fifth person who's a writer herself said the dialogue between the two leads in chapter 3 sounds too similar to each other. I don't really know what to do with any of this or whether I should keep working on it.
evals.expected_output: Unlike the previous version of this eval, the author here states no rule, no threshold, and no methodology of their own -- they just dump five raw, differently-shaped signals (a repeated-edit pattern, two pieces of praise, one specific-but-solo complaint, one vague-and-solo complaint, one mechanically checkable-but-solo complaint) and ask what to do. This tests whether the skill causes the assistant to *supply* a structured triage (freeze/evidence-doctrine style reasoning) unprompted, rather than just being able to follow a rule the user already wrote down (which the earlier version of this eval showed is something Claude already does well without the skill). A good response should: (1) name the repeated small-edit pattern on one paragraph as a stop/freeze-type signal on its own initiative, (2) NOT treat all five pieces of feedback as equally-weighted opinions to average or vote on, (3) differentiate the villain-motivation and chapter-3-dialogue-similarity comments (solo but conceptually specific and checkable) from the chapter-7 comment (solo and vague, not yet actionable) rather than treating all three solo reports identically, (4) propose a concrete test for at least the dialogue-similarity claim (e.g. a blind/anonymized comparison) rather than vague reassurance, and (5) not let the two positive pacing comments function as blanket permission to stop scrutinizing the rest of the book.
assertions: Response identifies the repeated small-edit pattern on the chapter 3 paragraph (eight times) as a stop/diminishing-returns signal on its own initiative, without the user having named any such rule or the word 'freeze' themselves
Response treats the villain-motivation comment and the chapter-3 dialogue-similarity comment as worth investigating/testing rather than dismissing either as 'just one opinion'

Response treats the vague 'chapter 7 felt off, can't say what' comment differently from the other two solo complaints -- as not yet actionable on its own, to be logged/watched for convergence rather than acted on or investigated immediately

Response proposes a concrete test-based approach for the chapter 3 dialogue-similarity claim specifically (e.g. a blind/anonymized dialogue comparison), not just general reassurance or a vague suggestion to 'look into it'

Response does not treat all five pieces of feedback as equally-weighted opinions to average, and does not let the two positive pacing comments function as a reason to stop scrutinizing the rest of the manuscript

evals.prompt: I have a three-page character bio for my protagonist -- her childhood, her family, where she went to school, her favorite foods, how her parents raised her, a whole backstory about a car accident when she was twelve. I know her better than any character I've ever written. But when I put her on the page in actual scenes, she still feels flat -- readers say she's 'fine' but forgettable. What am I missing?
evals.expected_output: This tests Phase 3 (characters) specifically, in a scenario chosen because the naive/generic craft-advice move -- and a very common piece of writing advice in general -- is to recommend adding MORE backstory detail, sensory specificity, or a distinctive quirk. The skill explicitly warns against this ('deconseiller les fiches biographiques encyclopediques -- illusion de profondeur') and redirects toward present-tense, choice-driven character construction: what she wants right now (not history), what she refuses to see or wrongly believes, what she hides, and critically what she would actually do under pressure/in a forced choice -- a character becomes vivid through choices under constraint, not volume of biographical information. A good response should diagnose the actual mismatch (bio depth =/= on-page vividness) rather than accepting the premise that more backstory work is the fix.
assertions: Response explicitly identifies that the amount/detail of backstory is not the cause of the flatness, rather than recommending the user add more backstory or biographical detail
Response reframes character construction around what she wants right now, in-scene, rather than her history
Response raises some version of self-deception, wrongful belief, or concealment (what she refuses to see / believes wrongly / hides) as more character-defining than biographical facts
Response emphasizes what the character would actually do under pressure or a forced choice as a test of character, not just interiority or backstory
Response does not recommend expanding or adding to the three-page bio document as the primary fix
